items.headline: Cadets get hurt about as often as soldiers in initial training, a USARIEM-led review finds
items.blurb: A scoping review led by USARIEM researchers pooled 34 US studies of service academy and ROTC cadets, covering cohorts of 27 to 24,501, and put every injury rate on the same scale. Academy cadets averaged 53.7 musculoskeletal injuries per 1,000 person-weeks and ROTC cadets 30.6. Most injuries were in the lower body, and female cadets had higher rates. Only 10 of the 34 studies were rated moderate quality, so for strength coaches, PTs and ATs working with pre-commissioning programs this is a starting benchmark and a case for better injury surveillance, not a final number.

items.headline: Night-owl veterans carry heavier PTSD, depression and insomnia symptoms
items.blurb: In 144 post-9/11 US veterans from a multi-site post-deployment health registry, evening types reported worse depression, PTSD, insomnia severity and sleep quality than morning types after adjusting for age and sex, and the link was not explained by how long they slept. Chronotype was not tied to trauma-associated sleep disturbance. It is a small cross-sectional sample, but for performance psychologists and H2F sleep staff it is a cheap screening cue: asking about sleep timing, not just duration, may flag who carries more symptom burden and who may respond differently to CBT-I.

items.headline: IACP opens speaker proposals for its 2027 Officer Safety and Wellness Conference
items.blurb: The International Association of Chiefs of Police is taking proposals for the 2027 OSW Conference, March 5-7 in Chicago, through October 16 at 11:59 p.m. CT. Topics include injury prevention, physical fitness, nutrition, sleep, peer support, suicide prevention and resilience. It is the main US stage for police wellness practitioners, so coaches, dietitians and clinicians with agency results should submit.

items.headline: IACP 2026 meets in Orlando 24 to 27 October
items.blurb: The International Association of Chiefs of Police annual conference runs 24 to 27 October 2026 at the Orange County Convention Center in Orlando, with four days of education workshops and an exhibit hall of more than 600 vendors. It expects more than 16,000 public safety professionals. For police wellness, fitness and performance providers, it is the biggest room of law enforcement decision-makers this year, and the exhibit hall is where departments shop for programs.

items.headline: FDIC 2027 registration opens 5 October for the April show in Indianapolis
items.blurb: FDIC International says attendee registration for its 12 to 17 April 2027 event in Indianapolis opens 5 October at noon ET. Conference passes start at $690, and summits, including EMS Innovation and Women in Fire, can be added. The 2026 show drew more than 38,000 attendees. The program is mostly fire operations, but for fire-service wellness and performance staff it is the largest fire-service gathering of the year for meeting departments.

items.headline: Neuromuscular training during recruit training cuts injuries; load management alone did not
items.blurb: A JOSPT meta-analysis pooled 33 studies and 49,062 military, police and fire recruits. Neuromuscular training delivered during recruit training reduced medical-attention injuries without raising attrition. Programs started before training did not reduce injuries and may have increased dropout, and load management alone showed no clear benefit. The evidence is very low certainty, but it backs embedding progressive neuromuscular work inside the academy schedule instead of bolting it on beforehand.

items.headline: Heavy-weapons training blast changes memory, gait and brain biomarkers within hours
items.blurb: The five-year INVICTA study followed 224 special operators, controls and range instructors through heavy-weapons training with blast gauges. Within minutes of firing, operators showed changes in short-term memory, EEG complexity and blood tau and UCH-L1, and gait and eye-movement changes appeared within hours. More than 20% had a hearing threshold shift. Effects were mostly short-lived, but instructors with repeated exposure over two-year tours had larger and longer-lasting changes, a direct input to exposure limits and to scheduling cadre on ranges.

items.headline: Six in ten first-term Sailors and Marines on limited duty leave service early
items.blurb: Among 22,500 enlisted Sailors and Marines who entered temporary limited duty (LIMDU) in their first contract (FY2017-2022), more than 60% left before finishing their service obligation, most often for medical disability. Entering LIMDU for mental or behavioral health conditions predicted worse outcomes than entering for musculoskeletal injury or pain. Marines did better than Sailors. The results raise questions about how often LIMDU returns people to full duty, which is where embedded rehab and performance teams can make a difference.

items.headline: Review finds too little evidence to write diet rules for shift workers, firefighters included
items.blurb: A systematic review of 43 studies on nutrition interventions for shift workers, with a pre-specified look at first responders, found the evidence too heterogeneous and biased to support formal dietary guidelines. Only about 9% of studies included firefighters or police; common interventions were macronutrient changes, time-restricted eating and meal timing. Dietitians working with 24-hour crews should treat shift-work nutrition advice as practice-based rather than settled, and there is room for well-designed station-based trials.

items.headline: EMS physicians say clinician mental health is a system problem, not a personal one
items.blurb: The National Association of EMS Physicians published a position statement calling EMS clinician mental health foundational to workforce sustainability and patient safety. It asks leaders to build mental health into EMS education, guarantee confidential and culturally competent care for medics, dispatchers, officers and firefighters, run quality improvement on practices that drive distress, and push for legislation and research partnerships. For performance psychologists and program leaders, this is the specialty's own medical directors endorsing embedded, confidential behavioral health support, which is a hiring argument agencies can cite.

items.headline: Officer deaths down 19% through September, but traffic deaths are up 48%
items.blurb: The National Law Enforcement Officers Memorial Fund's preliminary count shows 68 officer line-of-duty deaths from January 1 to October 1, 2026, versus 84 in the same period of 2025. Firearms deaths fell 34% (23 vs 35), but traffic-related deaths rose 48% (31 vs 21) and are now the leading cause. For trainers and program leaders, that shifts the safety conversation toward driving, fatigue and roadside exposure.

items.headline: Slow ruck times at Special Forces selection flag who gets hurt, sick or separated over the next two years
items.blurb: USARIEM followed 792 Special Forces Assessment and Selection candidates for two years after they enrolled, whether they passed or not. Slower road march times at enrollment came with 25-66% higher odds of injury, behavioral health diagnoses, sleep disorders and separation from service. More resistance training, better sleep quality and higher protein intake came with 18-45% lower odds of injury, and low mood, poor sleep and thin social support each raised the odds of separation by about 30%. For SOF strength coaches, dietitians and performance psychologists, this backs screening and building load-carriage capacity, lifting, sleep and protein before a candidate shows up at selection.

items.headline: Heavier World Trade Center exposure tracks with a thinner cortex in responders at midlife
items.blurb: Stony Brook researchers scanned 218 World Trade Center responders and unexposed controls aged 44 to 65 and found that a higher neurotoxicant exposure severity score went with thinner cortex across much of the brain, focused in precentral regions, even after adjusting for other factors. It is a cross-sectional imaging study and cannot prove cause, but it adds structural brain evidence to the cognitive-decline findings already reported in this group. For fire and rescue program leaders and medical staff, it strengthens the case for respiratory protection and exposure tracking at large incidents as long-term brain-health measures, not only lung and cancer measures.

items.headline: Hegseth says an equipment-free PT test is coming to every service and touts testosterone testing
items.blurb: In his first annual State of the Force address at Quantico, Secretary Hegseth recapped the year's fitness changes: male-standard scoring and a Combat Field Test for every combat MOS, two PT tests and two body-composition checks a year, and PT every duty day. He also said that soon every service will use a PT test 'that can be done with only a stopwatch and a clipboard,' speaking directly to the Army and adding 'no more mobile gym needed.' No directive has been published yet, so the equipment-free test is announced, not issued. If it arrives, Army programming built around the deadlift, sled and kettlebell events will have to change, so watch for an Army directive.

items.headline: Gynecomastia: 22,000 service members and $90 million in care over a decade
items.blurb: A Military Health System analysis found 22,103 active-duty men were diagnosed with gynecomastia from 2014 to 2023 (2.0 per 1,000 person-years, highest in the Marine Corps at 2.9). Nearly 38% had surgery, most within six months of diagnosis, and total costs were at least $90 million. The paper does not assess causes, but it gives men's health and performance staff a baseline for a condition linked to hormones, supplements and anabolic agents in young male populations.

items.headline: FEMA pushes $648 million in fire grants out the door, including $324 million for staffing
items.blurb: FEMA announced it awarded $648 million over the past week to more than 1,600 fire departments and first responder organizations through the FY2025 fire grant programs: $291.6 million in Assistance to Firefighters Grants, $324 million in SAFER staffing grants to nearly 200 departments, and $32.4 million in Fire Prevention and Safety grants. AFG money can fund health and wellness initiatives and protective gear, and FP&S funds research on firefighter safety, health and well-being. This is a hiring signal: SAFER dollars pay firefighter salaries, and AFG wellness awards are how many departments stand up physicals, peer fitness and performance-staff positions.

items.headline: Airmen and Guardians with high neuroticism score lower on VO2max, Wingate and endurance tests, and autonomy explains part of the gap
items.blurb: Researchers from AFIT and AFRL gave 186 active-duty Air Force and Space Force members personality and motivation surveys, then measured VO2max, Wingate anaerobic power and muscular endurance around a 12-week supervised training program. Higher neuroticism went with lower scores on all three tests and higher conscientiousness went with better aerobic capacity and endurance. Of the motivation measures, only a sense of autonomy predicted performance, and once autonomy was accounted for, neuroticism no longer predicted aerobic capacity or endurance. The mediation analysis was cross-sectional and the sample was one of convenience. Even so, it gives coaches and performance psychologists a reason to coach in an autonomy-supportive way, especially with anxious trainees on maximal-effort days.

items.headline: Only one in four Texas volunteer firefighters gets an annual medical exam
items.blurb: A survey of 326 Texas volunteer firefighters found just 26.4% receive an annual occupational health screening, despite NFPA recommendations. Cost was the top barrier, followed by not knowing where to go, lack of insurance, lack of providers and time; rural and full-time-employed volunteers reported more barriers. Since sudden cardiac events remain the leading on-duty killer, this frames where AFG wellness dollars and mobile screening programs for volunteer departments are most needed.

items.headline: One in three soldiers reports nightmares, insomnia or both before deploying
items.blurb: In 3,952 soldiers assessed before combat deployment (and 1,762 after), 12% had nightmares only, 9% insomnia only and 11% both. New-onset or chronic nightmare and insomnia trajectories after deployment tracked with higher PTSD, anger and anxiety symptoms. The authors argue for transdiagnostic treatment that targets both sleep problems together. For behavioral health and sleep staff, screening before deployment is the opportunity this study highlights.

items.headline: Cannabis use tracks with worse sleep in Guard and Reserve soldiers
items.blurb: A six-wave longitudinal study of 485 Army Reserve and National Guard soldiers found that current cannabis use was associated with worse global sleep quality. The strongest links were longer time to fall asleep (aIRR 1.15), more sleep disturbance and more use of sleep medication (aIRR 1.40). The findings cut against using cannabis as a sleep aid, a practice soldiers commonly report. They are useful context for reserve-component sleep education as state legalization spreads.

items.headline: Even a cool-lab 6-mile ruck leaves marchers dehydrated, with fatter marchers losing more
items.blurb: Sixteen load-carriage-experienced adults marched 9.65 km (6 miles) with a fighting load at 22 C without fluids. They lost about 1.5% of body mass and became mildly dehydrated. Fat mass and body fat percentage, but not aerobic fitness, correlated with larger changes in urine concentration. The authors urge researchers and trainers to measure and manage hydration even in mild conditions, a point that applies to heat-illness prevention planning.

items.headline: 97% of soldiers now have a cognitive baseline as the Army readies a blast overpressure directive
items.blurb: The Army reports that about 97% of soldiers have completed the Neurocognitive Assessment Tool (NCAT) baseline. Artillery, combat engineer and EOD soldiers must retest annually, and all other soldiers every three years. Officials said a service-wide blast overpressure directive is coming, covering exposure tracking, risk mitigation, cognitive monitoring, injury reporting and training. That program will need people to run cognitive monitoring and exposure tracking, so read it as a hiring signal for brain health and occupational health staff.

items.headline: A job-specific firefighter task test proves reliable enough to track moderate fitness changes
items.blurb: Brazilian researchers with Bond University's Tactical Research Unit tested a new simulated-task circuit (vehicle extrication plus structural fire suppression) twice in 21 career firefighters. The fire-suppression circuit and total time had excellent reliability (ICC above 0.9, CV under 5%) and could detect moderate, but not small, performance changes; the extrication circuit was less reliable. For coaches building job-related tests, it is a template for a defensible occupational test and a reminder to know a test's typical error before calling a change real.

items.headline: Three in four Brazilian military police officers show moderate-to-very-high burnout, and less active officers fare worse
items.blurb: A cross-sectional survey of 1,028 Brazilian Military Police officers found that 75.4% scored moderate to very high on the Burnout Assessment Tool. Burnout was higher among women, officers on fixed shifts, those on long-term medication or with prior psychological care, and those who were physically inactive. It is one country's force and a single snapshot, but the inactivity link gives police wellness and fitness staff another reason to count on-duty training time as part of a mental-health strategy.

items.headline: Women in uniform face 28% higher odds of overuse injury, and junior officers stand out
items.blurb: A Military Health System cohort of 624,842 injured service members (2017-2022) found women had 28% higher odds of non-acute musculoskeletal injury, with more stress fractures and overuse injuries but fewer fractures and dislocations. Female junior officers were 78% and 56% more likely than male peers to have acute and non-acute injuries. Women in Navy and health care jobs were also at higher risk. The study points injury-prevention staff toward specific subgroups, and junior officers are a group many programs overlook.

items.headline: SOF operators carry more lean mass, not less fat, than conventional units
items.blurb: In 500 Belgian male soldiers measured with multifrequency bioimpedance, special operations personnel had the highest fat-free mass index (21.0 kg/m2) while their fat mass index matched other units. PT instructors had the lowest body fat (13.7%) and frigate sailors the highest (19.7%). Over half of SOF combined low fat mass with high lean mass. The authors suggest lean-mass indices, not weight or BMI, as the more useful body composition marker in selection.

items.headline: GAO: civilian cuts left remote bases struggling to staff health care and other support
items.blurb: GAO found that remote and isolated installations struggle to recruit and keep the civilians who deliver health care, housing and other critical support. Eielson AFB alone had 428 vacant positions. DOD's civilian workforce reductions since January 2025 made staffing harder, and DOD has not assessed their effect at these sites. GAO recommends a clear definition of 'remote and isolated' and a lessons-learned review, and DOD concurred. For job seekers, these hard-to-fill locations are an opening.

items.headline: A meal-replacement shake plan cut body fat in overweight career firefighters
items.blurb: In a cluster-randomized trial across 26 fire stations (51 firefighters, average BMI 33), two high-protein meal-replacement shakes a day for 14 weeks reduced DXA body fat by about 1 percentage point versus wait-list control. Protein and fiber intake rose, trunk fat and BMI fell, and heart-rate recovery after a weighted stair climb improved, though stair-climb time and blood lipids did not change. Adherence was about 91% and crews found it convenient, which makes this a practical option dietitians and station fitness staff can actually run on shift.

items.headline: Workplace violence hits three in four emergency clinicians worldwide, and half get no prevention training
items.blurb: An 81-country survey of 1,306 emergency department and EMS professionals found 75% witnessed workplace violence in the past year, 40% reported physical harm and 69% psychological harm, mostly from patients, with intoxication and crowding as the main drivers. Only 51% had formal violence-prevention training and 57% had access to psychosocial support afterward. For EMS program leaders, the gap is concrete: de-escalation training and post-incident support are missing for roughly half the workforce.

items.headline: A crisis counselor inside the 911 center cut police suicide calls in Mesa
items.blurb: Embedding a crisis line specialist at Mesa, Arizona's 911 center was linked to 22 to 48 fewer police responses to suicide calls per 100,000 people per quarter versus a synthetic comparison built from 21 cities, about 230 to 490 officer hours saved each quarter. It shows mental health crisis work can be moved off patrol. Behavioral health staff embedded with police and dispatch are a hiring signal here.

items.headline: Air Force OST and True North teams merge into True North+ on 1 October
items.blurb: McConnell AFB's 22nd Medical Group Operational Support Team, made up of a physical therapist, a strength and conditioning coach, a psychologist, an LCSW and a team specialist, merged with the wing's True North mental-health and chaplain team into True North+ on 1 October. This is one installation's version of the Air Force-wide consolidation, which AFMEDCOM says reaches full operational capability in October 2026. After that, OST and True North staff sit under one wing special-staff function. For Air Force coaches and PTs, the reporting lines and program management office are changing, and AFMEDCOM's own update says the enterprise guidance arrives at FOC.

items.headline: H2F leaders say profiles are shorter and postpartum fitness returns faster in resourced brigades
items.blurb: At the Maneuver Warfighter Conference at Fort Benning on 16 and 17 September, the H2F director and USARIEM-linked health economist Tim Murray said musculoskeletal profiles run about five to six days shorter per injury with H2F. They also said soldiers in H2F-resourced brigades regain postpartum fitness scores about two months faster. Program directors described 24-hour access to injury-control teams in the 11th Airborne and drill-sergeant partnerships in basic training. The release also says the H2F Academy is moving to Fort Benning, with the complex fully operational in January 2027. For coaches, ATs and PTs, this is the ROI story the Army is using to justify further expansion, and expansion means more jobs.

items.headline: Turnout gear stops firefighters from lifting with a neutral spine
items.blurb: University of Toronto and Waterloo researchers, working with Toronto Fire, measured how far firefighters could reach toward the floor while their spine was blocked from flexing. Every gear component reduced reach depth, and full gear with boots cut it by about 12 cm compared with station wear. For strength coaches and PTs, the practical point is that 'hip hinge, keep your back straight' coaching taught in gym clothes may not be achievable in turnouts, so low-back injury prevention should train lifting strategies under the actual PPE constraint.

items.headline: IAFF warns members off multi-cancer blood tests being marketed to firefighters
items.blurb: The IAFF issued guidance saying no multi-cancer detection test is FDA-approved or Health Canada-authorized and that it does not recommend or endorse any of them. It notes companies are marketing these tests directly to firefighters, explains sensitivity, specificity and false-positive harms, and says the tests must not replace NFPA 1580 annual medical exams or USPSTF screenings. Department physicians and wellness coordinators fielding vendor pitches now have a union position to point to.

items.headline: Fallen Firefighters Foundation and Oklahoma State launch a firefighter survivability institute
items.blurb: Oklahoma State University and the National Fallen Firefighters Foundation launched the Institute for Firefighter Survivability on September 21, built on a three-year agreement signed in May, with TEEX, the Illinois Fire Service Institute and the First Responder Center for Excellence as partners. Its stated goal is to set a research agenda on the causes of firefighter deaths and injuries and push findings into training and daily department practice. Watch it as a new home for applied health and cardiac-prevention research, and a possible source of research and curriculum roles.

items.headline: Air medical crews lose measurable hearing over a single shift
items.blurb: Audiometry on 18 helicopter EMS crew members across 236 tests showed hearing thresholds worsening over a duty day, with the biggest shift in medical crew who wore no added hearing protection (6.8 dB) versus pilots (1.9 dB) and protected medics (0.5 dB). Losses concentrated in high frequencies, and the authors say helmets alone may not be enough. Programs supporting flight medics should treat double hearing protection as standard PPE, not an option.

items.headline: Six in ten Austrian EMS staff report second-victim distress after bad calls
items.blurb: A nationwide survey of 1,171 nonphysician EMS personnel in Austria found 60% had a second-victim experience, most often after unexpected patient death or suicide (42%) or aggression from patients or relatives (19%). High symptom burden was tied to call volume, paid rather than volunteer work, and, most strongly, seeking help and not getting it (odds ratio about 6). The practical takeaway for performance psychologists is that low-threshold peer support with structured follow-up is the obvious target.

items.headline: Pairing heart-rate wearables with heat sensors helps read firefighter strain during live fire
items.blurb: Duke engineers built a wireless system that syncs physiological and environmental sensors and tested it on 28 firefighters doing repeated warm-up and live-fire training circuits. It told warm-up from live-fire phases with over 97% accuracy, and a personalized model predicted self-rated wellness with a mean error of about 0.66 on a 10-point scale. A key finding for anyone running monitoring programs: vital signs alone did not explain how firefighters felt, as individual differences drove most of the variance.

items.headline: Stress and impulsivity scores did not predict who learns to shoot well at a federal police academy
items.blurb: Following 205 Brazilian Federal Police trainees through a 13-week firearms course, impulsivity, perceived stress and self-control scores did not predict early scores, rate of improvement or final marksmanship. Early live-fire performance was the best predictor of final results. For academy staff, that argues for early skill testing and coaching over psychological screening when it comes to firearms progression.

items.headline: Wearables catch blood-pressure drops in half of ceremonial guards during long standing
items.blurb: Researchers fitted 30 soldiers on State Ceremonial and Public Duties with Astroskin wearables under full-dress uniform across three 2.5-hour parades. During an hour of motionless standing, half showed blood pressure drops meeting criteria for orthostatic hypotension, and estimated core temperature reached 38.6 C. Larger leg mass and lower body fat were linked to bigger drops. The study shows wearables can work under uniform and gives practitioners data for preventing fainting on parade.

items.headline: Forest Service waives wildland pay cap, adds hazard pay for prescribed fire and expands free therapy to 20 sessions
items.blurb: The Forest Service's Chief Fire and Safety Officer announced the wildland firefighter pay cap is waived through 2027 and that qualifying prescribed fire duties became eligible for hazardous duty or environmental pay differentials from September 20, 2026. The joint USDA-Interior Wildland Fire Therapy Service, now in its second year, referred 339 employees from January to July with an average wait under four days, and is expanding from 16 to 20 free sessions a year. For behavioral health providers and program leaders, it is a concrete sign the federal wildland health program is growing and using contracted clinical capacity.

items.headline: Soldiers with embedded H2F teams get back from MSK injuries faster, 1.4-million-injury JAMA study finds
items.blurb: A USARIEM-led cohort study of 1.42 million musculoskeletal injuries in active-duty soldiers (FY18 to FY25) found that soldiers in brigades with Holistic Health and Fitness teams spent 5.9% fewer days on limited duty. The gain was bigger for lower-body injuries (6.9%) than upper-body injuries (3.8%). H2F soldiers were slightly more likely to be put on a profile in the first place, which the authors read as earlier access to care rather than more injuries. The authors estimate 3.3 to 4.0 million workdays restored, worth $93 to $164 million a year, which makes this the strongest outcome evidence yet for embedding PTs, ATs, strength coaches and dietitians with brigades as the Army works toward full H2F coverage by 2029.

items.headline: Ketone supplement preserved shooting performance during four nights of half sleep
items.blurb: In a double-blind crossover RCT, 32 adults (16 women) slept about 4 hours a night for four nights while taking a 25 g ketone precursor or placebo. The ketone drink raised blood ketones above 1.0 mM, added 13% more deep sleep, and improved virtual-reality shooting: an 8% better Hit Factor, 7% faster completion and slightly higher accuracy. The trial is small, but it gives dietitians and performance staff an early signal on a countermeasure for sleep restriction.

items.headline: A five-minute daily drill cut ankle sprains by more than half in infantry recruits
items.blurb: In a quasi-experimental study of infantry recruit cohorts, a daily 5-minute, equipment-free balance, agility and strength routine run for 12 weeks lowered ankle sprain incidence from 31.0% to 13.1%. Injured recruits in the program also held their functional performance, while injured controls declined. The benefit was largest for recruits with a previous sprain. It is a cheap, scalable warm-up that strength coaches and ATs can drop into existing PT.

items.headline: Bipartisan bill would write the first OSHA health standard for wildland firefighters
items.blurb: The Wildland Firefighter Health and Safety Act (S.5433, with House companion H.R.10492) was introduced September 17 and referred to Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. It would codify the Federal Wildland Firefighter Health and Wellbeing Program, run a respiratory-protection pilot, require OSHA to issue an interim then final wildland firefighter health standard, and mandate paid duty time to shower and decontaminate gear after smoke or PFAS exposure. It is only introduced, but if it moves it creates permanent health-program billets and exposure-control work that federal fire programs will need clinicians and program staff to run.

items.headline: PFAS levels and years on the job track with ALS-linked blood markers in firefighters
items.blurb: In 608 active-duty municipal and airport firefighters across 10 states, incumbents showed altered expression in ten ALS-related microRNAs compared with recruits, and more years of service tracked with lower expression of several. In a 302-person subset, higher serum PFAS (including PFOS, PFNA and PFHxS) was associated with 13 PFAS-microRNA links, six surviving correction for multiple testing. It is a cross-sectional biomarker signal, not proof of ALS risk, but it adds to the case for limiting PFAS exposure from gear and foam.

items.headline: Poor sleep is the link between police work stress and lower life satisfaction
items.blurb: A survey of 803 frontline officers in southeast China found work stress lowered life satisfaction directly and through a chain of weaker social support leading to worse sleep. Sleep disturbance sat in the middle of the pathway. For wellness programs, it supports pairing peer and family support with sleep coaching rather than treating them separately.

items.headline: Blast injury linked to diabetes, heart disease, seizures and stroke years after service
items.blurb: A Millennium Cohort study of 36,641 veterans using VA care found that self-reported blast injury during service was associated with higher rates of new diagnoses including seizures (APR 1.79), stroke (1.35), angina (1.43), diabetes (1.28) and neuropathy (1.38). Occupational risk of low-level blast was not associated with the same pattern. The authors frame blast as a long-term occupational health risk that reaches beyond the brain, which matters for anyone planning long-term health monitoring of blast-exposed career fields.

items.headline: Knee, back and shoulder pain drive most medical discharges of Danish conscripts
items.blurb: Of 17,579 Danish conscripts (2019-2023), 8.5% were medically discharged, a median of 5.4 weeks into service. Musculoskeletal conditions made up 80% of discharges for physical reasons, led by knee, back and shoulder pain. About a third were pre-existing, 37% overuse and 24% acute trauma. Because so many cases were pre-existing or overuse, the study points to accession screening and early load progression as the levers to pull.

items.headline: Diesel pollutants drift from engine bays into fire station living areas
items.blurb: University of Cincinnati researchers put low-cost air monitors in three fire stations for a week. NO2, VOCs and CO2 levels were tied to engine activity, distance from exhaust and station design, and measurable pollutants showed up beyond the apparatus bay in occupied spaces. Program leaders working on station design or exposure reduction can use this to justify exhaust capture and ventilation upgrades, which are fundable AFG items.

items.headline: Depression and PTSD symptoms connect differently in female and male firefighters
items.blurb: A network analysis of 6,240 Chinese firefighters (883 women) found women scored higher on both PTSD and depression. Fatigue, suicidal thoughts and sleep problems bridged the two conditions overall, but the bridges differed: fatigue and poor concentration in women, motor slowing and suicidal thoughts in men. Performance psychologists and peer support leads can use this to tailor screening questions and follow-up by sex.

items.headline: National Registry opens the LIFE Study, a long-term health cohort for EMS clinicians and firefighters
items.blurb: The National Registry of EMTs launched the website for the Longitudinal Inquiry into Fire and EMS Health (LIFE) Study, which will follow EMS clinicians and firefighters over their careers to see how exposures, injuries, workplace violence and stress add up to cardiovascular disease, cancer and mental health disorders. Partners include Ohio State, EMNet, NDRI, the University of Arizona and USU. It is not recruiting yet, but there is a sign-up for participation updates. This is the first large longitudinal look at EMS health, and the research team build-out is a modest hiring signal for occupational health researchers.

items.headline: Civilian police staff may carry hidden PTSD risk relative to sworn officers
items.blurb: A survey of 560 Norwegian Police Service employees found sworn officers had far more occupational trauma exposure (72% vs 22%), yet once exposure was accounted for, civilian employees had markedly higher odds of probable PTSD. The authors read it as sworn officers being better buffered, through selection, training or support, than the civilians who work beside them. Wellness programs that serve only sworn staff are probably missing a vulnerable group.

items.headline: Doing CPR in a moving ambulance drives low-back and wrist pain and worse compressions
items.blurb: In a simulation with 30 EMS providers, median pain jumped from 0 to 4 out of 10 after CPR in a moving ambulance, mostly in the lumbar spine and wrists, and compression quality dropped compared with a stationary setting. Providers worked in more trunk and elbow flexion and described balance and safety problems. Strength coaches and PTs working with EMS can use this to justify trunk, hip and wrist conditioning and to support the case for mechanical CPR devices on transport.

items.headline: US medics describe alcohol as the default way EMS crews bond and decompress
items.blurb: Interviews with 31 providers from non-fire-based EMS agencies across the US found alcohol functions as social glue, stress relief and informal coping in EMS culture. The authors argue any alcohol program has to work with those workplace norms rather than just targeting individuals. Dietitians and wellness leads can use this to frame alternatives that keep the social bonding and drop the drinking.

items.headline: Four in ten Polish officers report high exhaustion, and one day off a week makes it worse
items.blurb: A 2025 survey of 363 officers in Poland's Silesian region found 40% with high psychophysical exhaustion and 50% with disillusionment with work. Poor workplace relationships, bullying and lack of team support were the main risk factors, and officers with only one day off per week had significantly higher exhaustion. Recovery time is a schedule decision, and this gives program leaders data to argue for it.

items.headline: Air Mobility Command wing buys holistic health and fitness support for its contingency responders
items.blurb: The 621st Contingency Response Wing at JB McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst amended its Holistic Health and Fitness Support solicitation on 9 and 10 September, posting an updated performance work statement and Q&A. The work targets readiness, physical and non-physical performance, lower injury rates, better rehabilitation after injury, and mindfulness. Quotes were due 14 September under a total small-business set-aside. For coaches, ATs and mental-performance staff, this is another Air Force wing contracting its own performance team outside the medical group, so watch for the winning vendor's hiring.

items.headline: FEMA publishes how it scored this year's $291.6M firefighter grants, with wellness-fitness changes ahead
items.blurb: FEMA's 10 September Federal Register notice lays out the FY2025 Assistance to Firefighters Grant process: 8,426 applications for $291.6 million and roughly 1,800 awards, plus $32.4 million for Fire Prevention and Safety research grants. For future cycles, FEMA plans to limit Wellness and Fitness money to exercise equipment, physical evaluations and formal fitness program development. It will also add scored questions on need and an unscored question on how departments will sustain the program. Departments, and the coaches and dietitians they contract, should start building sustainability plans and needs data now.

items.headline: Officer burnout linked to a measurable epigenetic change in a brain-health gene
items.blurb: In 134 Brazilian public safety professionals, higher burnout scores tracked with lower DNA methylation at the BDNF exon IV promoter, independent of depression and anxiety, and female officers reported more burnout. BDNF supports neuroplasticity, so this is an early biological marker of chronic occupational stress. It is cross-sectional, but it adds weight to treating burnout as a physiological load, not a mood problem.

items.headline: Prescription nightmare-interrupting wearable showed early benefit in San Francisco police and firefighters
items.blurb: In an open-label pilot of 10 San Francisco first responders with PTSD, the FDA-authorized NightWare device cut nightmare frequency from 5.2 to 3.6 nights a week and nightmare distress by more than half over 60 days, with no one getting worse. Use averaged 76% of nights. It is tiny and uncontrolled, but it is one of few nightmare treatments tested in this population.

items.headline: Oregon Air Guard awards $2.5M human performance contract for its Special Tactics squadron
items.blurb: On 9 September the Oregon Air National Guard awarded Duro Health LLC a $2.54 million contract (base plus options) for a Human Performance Program supporting the 125th Special Tactics Squadron in Portland. The scope covers physical therapy and injury management, athletic training, strength and conditioning, and cognitive performance, with a focus on return-to-duty speed. For PTs, ATs and coaches, it is a live contractor team to watch for openings. It also shows Guard special-tactics units buying SOF-style embedded performance support on their own.

items.headline: Army special operations school scouts wearables to watch candidates' vitals during selection
items.blurb: USSOCOM, on behalf of the Army's Special Warfare Center and School, re-posted a request for information on 8 September, with responses due 17 September. It seeks wearables that track core temperature and heart rate, location and two-way communication for every ARSOF candidate in assessment, selection, qualification and PME courses. The stated drivers are heat injury, cardiac events, dehydration and hypothermia occurring out of cadre sight. The RFI asks for AI-enabled dashboards covering 400 or more devices. For performance and medical staff, this points to real-time physiological monitoring becoming part of selection safety, and to more data for someone to interpret.

items.headline: 'Operator Syndrome' still lacks a definition, scoping review warns
items.blurb: A PRISMA-ScR review found only six sources (2020-2026) that explicitly define Operator Syndrome among U.S. special operations forces, and only two were empirical. The construct is consistently described as the combined burden of blast, repeated mild TBI, chronic musculoskeletal loading, sleep disruption and sustained stress. For SOF performance and medical teams, the takeaway is that the label is widely used but validated assessment tools and outcome data are still missing.

items.headline: Meta-analysis confirms caffeine protects vigilance and task performance under sleep loss
items.blurb: Pooling seven double-blind placebo-controlled trials in military or military-like populations, this review found acute caffeine improved vigilance (SMD 0.73), complex cognition (SMD 0.54) and military task performance (SMD 0.45) during sleep deprivation or restriction. The effect showed up mostly as faster task execution. It is the first quantitative synthesis of a tool most units already use, and dietitians and performance coaches can cite it when building caffeine guidance for sustained operations.

items.headline: Drone crews' stressors are mostly organizational, not combat, review finds
items.blurb: A PROSPERO-registered systematic review of 14 studies on military remotely piloted aircraft crews found probable PTSD in 3.3-6.7%, emotional exhaustion in 25-37% and suicidal ideation in 4.4-8.0%. The main risk factors were long hours, unstable shifts, understaffing and sleep disruption rather than combat exposure. As drone forces grow, the review points performance psychologists and leaders toward schedule and staffing fixes, not only individual resilience training.

items.headline: Full kit adds about 15 kg and changes how tactical officers sense their own bodies
items.blurb: In 15 Brazilian special operations police officers, operational uniform and PPE added about 14.8 kg and raised musculoskeletal discomfort across most body regions compared with PT gear. Officers also underestimated their own body dimensions in kit, a shift in body schema that could affect movement and spacing. Small study, but it gives strength coaches a reason to train and test in loaded kit, not just gym clothes.

items.headline: Cardiologists publish the first playbook for clearing firefighters, cops and soldiers with heart conditions
items.blurb: The ACC and AHA released a joint scientific statement on caring for tactical athletes with cardiovascular disease, published simultaneously in JACC and Circulation. It introduces 'Tactical Clinical Management', a framework that weighs a responder's heart condition against the actual task demands and the risk sudden incapacitation poses to the crew, across 11 sections from preparticipation ECG screening to the older tactical athlete. For fire department physicians, PTs and program leads this is now the reference document when a firefighter with a cardiac finding needs a fit-for-duty call, and it pairs screening with practical steps like AED access during timed fitness testing.

items.headline: Army Reserve is about to bid out a 25-person H2F performance team
items.blurb: The Army Reserve posted a pre-solicitation on 3 September for a contractor-run Holistic Health and Fitness Performance Team: 25 full-time registered dietitians, cognitive performance specialists, strength and conditioning coaches and athletic trainers. They would be spread across ten sites, including Pinellas Park, Fort McCoy, Fort Snelling, JB McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst and Fort Jackson. The work is non-clinical: command-specific readiness programs, coaching, education and mentoring unit H2F integration teams, with evening and weekend hours to fit drill schedules. This is a clear hiring signal for reserve-component H2F. The single-award IDIQ runs a 12-month base plus an option, it is a small-business set-aside, and the full solicitation was expected within weeks.

items.headline: DHA orders testosterone screening for men 30 and older and RED-S screening for all women at annual health assessments
items.blurb: The Defense Health Agency turned the Secretary of War's July 15 health and human performance memo into clinical protocol. Male service members 30 and older are now screened for low testosterone at the annual Periodic Health Assessment with three symptom questions and a lab draw (optional under 30). A result under 300 ng/dL triggers a confirmatory LC/MS test and workup, and when a BMI of 27 or more drives the low testosterone, a 5-10% weight-loss lifestyle program comes first or runs alongside replacement therapy. Women of any age are screened for RED-S (fatigue, MSK pain, cycles longer than 35 days), and women 35 and older for perimenopause and menopause symptoms that affect duty. Dietitians and performance staff should expect referrals, because the guidance names caloric deficit, sleep loss and training stress as reversible causes and says levels usually recover within 4-7 days of adequate fuel, 7-9 hours of sleep and training recovery.

items.headline: Caffeine gum sharpened firefighters' balance in full gear after a GABA dose
items.blurb: In a double-blind crossover trial, 14 elite Taiwanese firefighters took GABA and then chewed caffeinated or caffeine-free gum before a functional balance test in about 25 kg of gear. The caffeine trial improved completion time and performance index with small-to-moderate effect sizes, alongside higher salivary alpha-amylase, a marker of sympathetic activity. The sample is tiny, but it is a useful note for sports dietitians on fast-acting caffeine for crews coming off rest.

items.headline: Blast-prone jobs carry 43% higher TBI and 39% higher hearing-injury rates (MSMR)
items.blurb: A September MSMR cohort compared 831,050 active-duty soldiers, airmen and Marines in occupations at high risk of blast overpressure with 2.2 million who never served in them. After adjustment, the high-risk group had higher incidence of TBI (aIRR 1.43) and noise-induced hearing injury (aIRR 1.39). Migraine incidence rose faster with time in those jobs. AFHSD calls for better exposure monitoring and hazard mitigation, which supports the case for embedded brain health monitoring in fires and EOD units.

items.headline: Skipping full meals in basic training doubled injury odds in Swedish conscripts
items.blurb: In 225 Swedish conscripts (96 women) followed through five months of basic combat training, those who regularly ate less than full meal portions had lower baseline work capacity and higher odds of injury or overuse symptoms (OR 2.33) and missed training (OR 1.85). Vegetarian patterns were linked to lower starting ferritin, and under-eating limited hemoglobin gains. The findings support fueling education and dining access as injury prevention, not only nutrition policy.

items.headline: Pentagon makes two fitness tests a year, male-standard combat scoring and a 0.55 waist-to-height cap permanent policy
items.blurb: The Pentagon reissued its fitness and body-composition instruction, folding last year's Secretary of War memos into standing policy. Active-duty troops now take two tests a year (their service test plus a Combat Field Test for the 80-plus combat-arms jobs listed, or a Combat Readiness Test for everyone else), combat arms score on the male standard and must average 70%, and everyone gets measured twice a year against a waist-to-height ratio under 0.55, with body-fat limits that can be no stricter than 18% for men and 26% for women and no looser than 26% and 36%. It also tells commanders to allow PT every duty day, gives a 12-month testing exemption after birth or pregnancy loss, sends anyone waived for more than 18 months for the same condition to be assessed for the Disability Evaluation System, and requires a medical evaluation for everyone entering remedial PT. For coaches, ATs and dietitians the big change is accountability: starting June 1, 2027 each service must report the science behind its tests plus its injury and test data, which is a lasting demand signal for performance staff.

items.headline: Resilience training helps first responders with stress short term, but evidence is thin
items.blurb: A Campbell systematic review of 220 trials found proactive resilience programs for high-risk occupations improved resilience and stress in the short term (SMD about 0.4), with smaller effects on anxiety, depression and PTSD symptoms. Only resilience and stress gains held up long term, certainty ranged from low to very low, and only 3% of comparisons involved firefighters or first responders. Performance psychologists should set realistic expectations for resilience programming and build evaluation into any rollout.

items.headline: SOCOM moves its operator nutrition app in-house, linking up to 55 dietitians to Smartabase
items.blurb: USSOCOM posted a sole-source combined synopsis/solicitation on 31 August to license Teamworks Nutrition, formerly Notemeal, from Teamworks Tactical Solutions. The license is a base year plus three option years. The platform must be FedRAMP IL4/IL5 and already have two-way integration with SOCOM's Human Performance Data Management System, Smartabase, so meal logs sit beside training and injury data. For performance dietitians, this confirms nutrition data is now part of the SOF human-performance data stack, and fluency with these platforms is part of the job.

items.headline: SOMA 2027 wants Human Performance and Resiliency talks, with submissions due 13 November
items.blurb: The Special Operations Medical Association's 2027 Scientific Assembly runs 26 to 30 April 2027 in Raleigh. Its call for labs, podium talks and research includes a Human Performance and Resiliency track and a Brain Health track. Submissions close 13 November 2026. SOMA is also NTOA's official tactical EMS conference, so a talk there reaches SOF medics and tactical police medics alike. For human performance staff with outcome data, this is a direct line to the SOF medical community.

items.headline: IAFF puts nearly 300 health and safety resources in one searchable library
items.blurb: On 28 August the IAFF launched a public Resource Library that gathers almost 300 of its reports, guides, checklists, trainings and webinars for fire fighters and EMS workers. It can be searched by topics such as nutrition and fitness, occupational cancer and building codes. For department wellness coordinators and contracted coaches or dietitians, it is now the fastest way to find the union's own Fit to Thrive and health guidance and to cite it in program plans.

items.headline: Review maps what mind-body and lifestyle programs have been tested in US police
items.blurb: A structured review found 21 studies of integrative interventions in US law enforcement, grouped into mindfulness, self-regulation, wellness programs, sleep, yoga and detoxification approaches, with outcomes ranging from stress and burnout to physiology, aggression and job performance. The authors flag the need for more rigorous trials. It is a handy evidence map for wellness coordinators choosing what to pilot.

items.headline: Swedish ambulance crews say their own reactions can set off violent encounters
items.blurb: Focus groups with 10 experienced Swedish ambulance personnel who had been assaulted found violence was more likely when crews lacked empathy, acted disrespectfully, reacted to provocation, or lost control of an unpredictable scene, often with intoxicated patients. The authors call for training to spot high-risk situations and de-escalate. It is a useful counterpoint for EMS trainers: violence prevention is partly a crew skill that can be coached.

items.headline: Army H2F has 90 performance teams fielded or in process, and Guard and Reserve models are next
items.blurb: The Army's H2F directorate reports 49 H2F Performance Teams and one Area Support Team fielded from FY21 to FY24, none in FY25 because of the civilian hiring freeze, and 41 more teams plus another AST now being fielded for FY25-26. That makes 90 teams and two ASTs fielded or in process. Each team puts physical therapists, strength coaches, athletic trainers, occupational therapists, dietitians and cognitive performance specialists inside a brigade, and FY27 fielding will lean toward Area Support Teams for smaller support units. The Army Reserve is building hub-and-spoke teams at its readiness divisions, and the Guard will place teams at state Joint Force Headquarters before switching to hub-and-spoke in FY28, so read this as a hiring signal with civilian and Title 32 roles opening across all three components.

items.headline: Paramedics value peer supporters who reach out first
items.blurb: Interviews with 13 Australian paramedics who recently used peer support found proactive outreach from peers overcame the reluctance to self-refer and helped identify at-risk staff. Shared experience drove the benefit, and matching the right peer to the right medic mattered. For agencies building peer programs, the design lesson is to budget for outreach and matching, not just a phone line.

items.headline: Job demands and role conflict track with poorer health in rural and urban ambulance crews
items.blurb: A survey of 134 ambulance clinicians in northern Sweden found 19% screened positive for anxiety and 13% for depression, with urban stations reporting higher demands, worse sleep and more posttraumatic stress than rural ones. Role clarity, job satisfaction, good leadership and a positive culture were protective. It points EMS leaders toward fixable organizational levers rather than only individual resilience training.

items.headline: NERIS Public puts near real-time fire incident data online for anyone
items.blurb: The U.S. Fire Administration launched NERIS Public: Incident Basics, a free ArcGIS dataset of incident-level fire data from NERIS, refreshed several times a week, with no login needed. It includes about 40 fields such as incident type, date, location and actions taken, but excludes casualty, medical and detailed unit data. It is not built for injury surveillance, but program leaders can now pull local call volume and type quickly when justifying staffing or wellness grants.

items.headline: Correctional officer health framed as an occupational risk chain from schedules to heart disease
items.blurb: A structured review of 69 sources proposes a pathway model for correctional officers: understaffing, overtime and unpredictable schedules drive sleep disruption, chronic stress and hypervigilance, which feed burnout, PTSD, suicide risk, cardiometabolic disease, musculoskeletal pain and fatigue. The authors argue for Total Worker Health strategies such as staffing and schedule reform, fatigue management and cardiometabolic screening over stand-alone resilience classes. It gives corrections wellness leads a framework for program design.

items.headline: Postpartum depression and anxiety diagnoses in servicewomen rose fivefold since 2010 (MSMR)
items.blurb: Among 138,588 active-duty women with a live birth, diagnosed postpartum depression or anxiety rose from 2.4% (2010-2015) to a peak of 13.4% in 2021-2022, then eased to 12.4% after parental leave expanded. Prior depression, anxiety or adjustment disorder, Navy service and cesarean delivery raised the odds. Officers had lower odds. AFHSD names prior mental health history as the main flag, which matters for postpartum return-to-fitness and behavioral health teams.

items.headline: Indiana switches every police academy to a job-task agility test
items.blurb: Starting August 1, 2026, the Indiana Law Enforcement Academy's Physical Agility Test replaced the old fitness battery as the statewide standard for all law enforcement, based on a job task analysis. The entrance standard is 4:08 and the exit standard 3:58, and ILEA posted the course diagram, equipment list, protocols and a pre-academy training manual with weighted-vest circuits. Coaches preparing Indiana recruits now train for a timed occupational course, not push-ups and a run.

items.headline: Meta-analysis: poor sleep and high stress travel together in police officers
items.blurb: A review of nine studies covering 7,550 police officers found poor sleep quality was linked to significantly higher perceived stress (SMD 0.76), and the relationship ran both ways. Heterogeneity was moderate. It firms up sleep as a core target for police wellness programs.

items.headline: AMSUS 2027 is set for 16 to 18 March, with abstracts due 30 October
items.blurb: AMSUS, the Society of Federal Health Professionals, will hold its 2027 annual meeting on 16 to 18 March at the Gaylord National in National Harbor, Maryland. Plenary, breakout and poster abstracts close 30 October 2026, and VA staff have earlier clearance steps. The meeting draws DoW, VA, HHS and DHS health leaders, so it is a venue for H2F, POTFF and TN+ outcome data to reach the people who fund those programs.

items.headline: Mental health diagnoses: over a million new ones in five years across the active force
items.blurb: This MSMR update counts 1,050,231 incident mental health diagnoses among 582,279 active-component members from 2021 to 2025, with a 2025 rate of 10,990.6 per 100,000 person-years after a 2023 peak. Adjustment, anxiety and depressive disorders make up 66.5% of diagnoses, and nearly half of those affected had diagnoses in more than one category. Health care personnel had the highest rates for most disorders and combat roles the most substance-related ones, which is a strong argument for embedded performance psychologists.

items.headline: Testosterone screening becomes a mandatory part of the annual health check for everyone 30 and over
items.blurb: A July 15 Secretary of War memo makes testosterone-deficiency screening a required element of the Periodic Health Assessment for all Active and Reserve personnel aged 30 and older, with under-30s able to request it. It ties the move to Human Performance Optimization and Operator Syndrome, orders DoDI 6200.06 updated by August 15, 2026, and stands up an external advisory council on health and human performance. Expect men's-health referrals, lab volume and questions about TRT and training to land on performance teams and clinicians fast.

items.headline: GAO: Army and Air Force still haven't updated field-hospital quality policies
items.blurb: GAO reports that, as of March 2026, the Army and Air Force had not issued the clinical quality management policies for operational settings that DoD ordered in 2023. These cover credentialing, patient safety and provider investigations on hospital ships and in field hospitals; the Navy has issued several. It matters mostly to deployed medical leaders, and only indirectly to performance teams.

items.headline: USU launches ARMORR to embed performance teams 'left of bang'
items.blurb: USU stood up ARMORR in May 2026 by merging its Center for Rehabilitation Sciences Research, CHAMP and the MIRROR MSK-injury program into one center. The new center embeds health and performance teams in operational units so injuries are prevented rather than treated later in clinics. Leaders from all four services backed the prevention-first approach at AMSUS, and a consolidated USU center with HPRC under it is a signal of future research and embedded-staff positions.

items.headline: Review: embedded SOF performance programs look effective but are poorly measured
items.blurb: This systematized narrative review searched 2010-2025 literature and kept 37 studies, 6 of which directly evaluated SOF HPO programs. Operators in embedded multidisciplinary programs showed better fitness scores, fewer self-reported injuries and higher training completion, but almost all of the evidence is nonrandomized. The authors say specialists working in parallel and the lack of shared metrics hold programs back, and they push for truly interdisciplinary teams with common protocols, which is useful framing for anyone designing an HPO evaluation.

items.headline: Army makes waist-to-height ratio its only body-composition standard
items.blurb: Army Directive 2026-13 drops height/weight tables and the tape test: WHtR is now the only authorized ABCP measure, taken at least twice a year, and anything at or above 0.55 means a same-day confirmation by a second team, then a flag and ABCP enrollment. No other body-fat method can be used to challenge the result, no AFT score exempts a soldier, and every soldier needs a WHtR recorded within 90 days of the directive. Commanders, not a designated NCO, now own the program, and units must leave at least 7 days between a fitness test and a WHtR, which matters for dietitians and H2F teams scheduling around test windows.

items.headline: MSK problems were the top reason deployed troops sought care in 2025
items.blurb: MSMR's annual deployed-morbidity report covers four combatant commands for the first time. In 2025, musculoskeletal conditions were the leading cause of in-theater care in AFRICOM, CENTCOM and SOUTHCOM, mental health led in PACOM, and CENTCOM accounted for almost 90% of encounters. The authors call for in-theater mental health assets and targeted MSK injury prevention, which is exactly the remit of deployable H2F-style teams.

items.headline: GAO snapshot: military health system still short of staff and readiness data
items.blurb: GAO's June 25 snapshot sizes the Military Health System at 9.4 million beneficiaries, 700+ facilities, more than 100,000 staff and over $72.5 billion expected in FY2027. It says DoD has not identified the resources or oversight its reforms need, and lacks key data and metrics on the clinical readiness of its medical personnel. Useful context for anyone pitching performance or MSK services into an MHS trying to pull care back into military facilities.

items.headline: USU sleep summit: most deployed troops get under seven hours, and leaders call it a readiness problem
items.blurb: At USU's Sleep and Fatigue Management Summit, co-hosted with WRAIR, the Air Force and DHA, presenters reported that nearly 85% of deployed service members sleep less than the recommended seven hours. DoW's acting Warfighter Performance Optimization director said most report six hours or less and compared that to the impairment of legal intoxication, and speakers described drone-era battlefields where safe rest areas no longer exist. The figures are as reported at the event, but the policy signal is plain: sleep is moving into readiness metrics, which helps anyone building fatigue-management programming.

items.headline: Navy app with dietitian review improves recruits' readiness before boot camp
items.blurb: Naval Health Research Center researchers put 92 Future Sailors in the Delayed Entry Program on the CoachMePlus app, which delivered military-training, nutrition and PT modules and had a registered dietitian review monthly food logs. Knowledge scores rose (nutrition from 58 to 69), 92% graduated basic training, and graduates scored higher on drill-instructor assessments, but logs showed low fibre, calcium and vitamin D and high fat and sodium. There was no control group, so treat it as a feasibility signal for remote pre-accession nutrition and fitness coaching.

items.headline: GAO: DoD can't say whether its civilian trauma-center partnerships keep medics ready
items.blurb: GAO found that DHA has no complete inventory of the partnerships that place military medical staff in civilian facilities to keep their clinical skills sharp. Neither DHA nor the services fully measure what those partnerships contribute to clinical readiness, and DoD has not looked at using resource-sharing agreements to cut costs. GAO made recommendations on inventory, data collection and cost-saving strategies.

items.headline: H2F Symposium: proponency moves to Fort Benning and the Guard pushes H2F to all 54 states and territories
items.blurb: At the May 12-14 H2F Symposium, the Army moved H2F proponency from the Center for Initial Military Training to the Maneuver Center of Excellence, with the H2F Academy and campus going to Fort Benning. The Guard said a four-state pilot is producing results and it is working to resource H2F in all 50 states and four territories. Best-in-Class awards went to teams such as 1st IBCT, 11th Airborne's Wolf Recovery program, which ran 149 on-the-spot injury evaluations after a JPMRC rotation. Guard and Reserve expansion is a clear hiring signal for strength coaches, ATs, dietitians and performance psychologists.

items.headline: Pentagon orders Warfighter Performance Optimization: cognition measured like fitness, wearables fast-tracked
items.blurb: This May 6 Secretary of War memo launches Warfighter Performance Optimization, a modernized take on Total Force Fitness that treats the warfighter as a readiness capability. It directs a rapid pipeline for wearables and data analytics, makes cognitive performance a core occupational readiness competency measured like physical standards, and pulls performance programs into one funded portfolio inside the budget process. P&R owes a 60-day assessment of existing initiatives, so program leaders should expect data calls now and new resourcing lines after; it reads as a hiring signal for performance and data roles.

items.headline: May MSMR: heat stroke up two years running, plus rhabdo, hyponatremia and a doubling of cold injuries
items.blurb: The May 2026 MSMR issue reports 2025 active-component heat stroke at 39.4 and heat exhaustion at 170.0 per 100,000 person-years. Heat stroke has risen for the second year in a row, and rates stay highest in under-20s, Marines, soldiers and recruits. The issue also updates exertional rhabdomyolysis and exertional hyponatremia, and its reportable-events review shows cold-weather injuries up 155% over 2024. For coaches and ATs this is the annual case for heat acclimatization, hydration and cold-weather plans in training pipelines.

items.headline: Space Force fitness manual moves to WHtR, a 2-mile run option and twice-yearly testing
items.blurb: Interim Change 3 to SPFMAN 36-2905, dated April 24, 2026, writes the September 2025 and December 2025 SecWar fitness memos into Space Force policy. The service's own announcement says every Guardian completes two Human Performance Assessments a year from January 1, 2026, even if enrolled in the Continuous Fitness Assessment. Cardio is a 2-mile run or the 20 m HAMR (at least one must be the run), with push-up, core and waist-to-height components, and scores are now on performance briefs.

items.headline: Army adds a pass/fail Combat Field Test for combat-arms soldiers
items.blurb: Army Directive 2026-07 makes the Combat Field Test a fitness requirement for soldiers in combat specialties: a continuous, pass/fail course of a 1-mile run, 30 dead-stop push-ups, 100 m sprint, 16 sandbag lifts to a 65-inch platform, a 50 m water-can carry, a 50 m crawl-and-rush drill and a second mile, in uniform and boots. Active-duty combat soldiers now take one CFT and one AFT for record each year, while other Reserve Component soldiers alternate. Soldiers whose permanent profiles keep them from AFT events face reclassification review, so coaches and ATs in combat brigades should plan for load-carriage and work-capacity prep, not just test-event training.

items.headline: Military surveillance case definition for testicular cancer refreshed
items.blurb: AFHSD's updated surveillance case definition (ONC 14) sets how the military counts testicular cancer in its epidemiology reports: one qualifying hospitalization or three outpatient encounters within 90 days, with ICD-9/10 code lists. Its background notes the cancer peaks between ages 15 and 35, which is the core of the force, and has over 95% five-year survival. It is a methods document for analysts, not screening guidance.

items.headline: Air Force rewrites its fitness test: 2-mile run, WHtR worth 20 points
items.blurb: The March 24, 2026 AFMAN 36-2905 is a full rewrite of the Air Force fitness program and supersedes the 2022 manual. The 1.5-mile run gives way to a 2-mile run or the 20 m HAMR, scoring becomes 50 points cardio, 15 strength, 15 core and 20 for waist-to-height ratio, and WHtR is measured apart from the other components to discourage unsafe cutting. Anyone coaching Airmen should rebuild aerobic prep around the longer run.

items.headline: Military suicides fell in 2024, but Guard rates rose
items.blurb: DoD's CY2024 Annual Report on Suicide in the Military counts 471 service member suicides (23.2 per 100,000), down from 531 in 2023. Active-component and Reserve rates fell, but the National Guard rate rose to 24.6, and active-component rates have climbed since 2011. Most deaths were enlisted men under 30, and two-thirds involved firearms, so lethal-means safety and support for young enlisted members remain the priorities for behavioral-health and performance teams.

items.headline: RAND maps a decade of military TBI research and finds it fragmented
items.blurb: This RAND scoping review maps military TBI research from January 2015 to June 2025 and finds the field still fragmented and siloed despite heavy federal and private investment. It notes more than 500,000 service members affected since 2000, with special operations forces at high risk from repeated blast exposure, and frequent overlap with PTSD and depression. It is a road map of gaps rather than new data, useful for program leaders arguing for blast-exposure monitoring and brain-health work.

items.headline: GAO tells Congress most of its readiness fixes remain open
items.blurb: In March 4 Senate testimony, GAO says U.S. readiness has degraded over two decades across air, sea, ground and space, mostly from sustaining old systems while buying new ones. Of nearly 200 recommendations, DoD still needs to act on more than 150. It is an equipment and sustainment story more than a human-performance one, so it is mostly background for program leaders framing readiness arguments.

items.headline: Marine Corps swaps height/weight for waist-to-height ratio and phases in BIA
items.blurb: MARADMIN 066/26 is Change 1 to MARADMIN 613/25, bringing the Corps in line with the December 2025 SecWar guidance: from January 1, 2026, waist-to-height ratio replaces the semiannual height-and-weight check, and only Marines over their maximum waist go on to a body-fat evaluation. Tape test and bioelectrical impedance remain the two body-fat methods, a Marine needs to pass only one, and BIA will fully replace the tape once devices are fielded Corps-wide. Marines scoring 285 or more on both PFT and CFT get up to 26% (men) or 36% (women) body fat; weight is still recorded in 2026 to study the change but is not used for evaluation.

items.headline: Orthopaedic leaders call for one integrated military MSK readiness effort
items.blurb: This Military Medicine commentary argues MSK injury is still the biggest threat to readiness, deployability and retention, and that the problem is fragmentation, not a lack of programs. The authors want the Society of Military Orthopaedic Surgeons, MAST, CHAMP and USU's MIRROR formally aligned with DHA and the service medical departments, with shared data from registries like MOTION guiding research. It is opinion rather than new data, but it shows where the MSK enterprise is heading organizationally.

items.headline: H2F performance teams return about $8 for every $1, says a 56-brigade study
items.blurb: This Sports Medicine study compares 28 brigades with H2F Performance Teams against 28 matched controls (over 1 million soldiers, FY2019-2023) using a difference-in-differences design. In brigades with teams, odds of MSK injury referral fell 61%, substance-abuse profiles 79%, long behavioral-health profiles 44% and ACFT failure 22%. Monte Carlo modelling puts the value at $24.4 million per brigade per year, an ROI of 8.15:1. It is observational and the dollar values are modelled, but it is now the main evidence for expanding the teams, and a strong hiring signal.

items.headline: CDMRP gets $1.27 billion across 34 programs for FY2026
items.blurb: The Consolidated Appropriations Act signed February 3 funds 34 CDMRP programs at $1.27 billion. Lines that matter for performance work include the Peer Reviewed Medical Research Program ($370M), TBI and Psychological Health ($40.5M), Orthopaedic ($20M), Joint Warfighter Medical ($10M), Military Burn ($10M) and Combat Readiness Medical ($5M). Funding announcements follow program by program, which puts grant and research-staff hiring 12-24 months out.

items.headline: TBICoE review: screen for PTSD whenever you evaluate mild TBI
items.blurb: TBICoE's research review on comorbid mild TBI and PTSD (current as of December 2025) finds service members are at higher risk of the pair, and that combat-related and blast-related TBIs carry worse PTSD outcomes. Its practical advice: screen for PTSD during every mild-TBI evaluation, expect more severe and lasting symptoms when both are present, and use integrated behavioral-health and rehab care. Performance psychologists and rehab staff will find it a good primer for coordinating care.

items.headline: CRS primer: the military health system's $64 billion budget and push to pull care back in-house
items.blurb: The January 14, 2026 update of CRS's Defense Primer on the MHS describes 9.4 million beneficiaries, 601 military treatment facilities and a $64.0 billion FY2026 Unified Medical Budget request, including $39.2 billion for the Defense Health Program. It highlights DoD's strategy to bring beneficiaries back to military facilities, where DoD currently buys more than 65% of care from the private sector. Handy background for program leaders explaining where H2F and MSK care sit in the MHS.

items.headline: Navy goes to two fitness cycles, daily PT and a one-time reset of past PFA failures
items.blurb: NAVADMIN 264/25 sets two PFA/CFA cycles for 2026 (January to June and July to December) and requires commands to fit PT into every workday. It wipes PFA failures before January 1, 2026 for advancement and retention decisions, while new failures now bring administrative action and fuller FITREP/EVAL documentation. Combat-arms sailors get an annual Combat Fitness Assessment, and body-composition assessment becomes a two-step process with a tighter high-performance exemption, so command fitness leaders and Navy performance staff have new program work.

items.headline: Army trial tests whole-person pain care against usual care for chronic MSK pain
items.blurb: The PROs trial, led by Brooke Army Medical Center with NCCIH and several Army and Air Force sites, started December 19, 2025 and is recruiting 608 MHS patients with chronic musculoskeletal pain. It randomizes them to usual care, Empowered Relief or Move to Health within a stepped-care design, using the EHR to drive recruitment and implementation. Primary completion is expected July 2027; there are no results yet, but it will shape how holistic pain care is delivered across the MHS.

items.headline: Waist-to-height ratio replaces height and weight tables across the joint force
items.blurb: This December 18, 2025 USW(P&R) memo sets the joint rule behind every service's new body-composition policy: from January 1, 2026, height/weight tables are out and waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) is in, checked twice a year with a ceiling below 0.55. Anyone at 0.55 or above gets a body-fat check, with service limits no stricter than 18%/26% and no looser than 26%/36% (men/women), and fails go to remedial programs and medical referral. High fitness scores can earn allowances but never excuse noncompliance; DoDI 1308.03 is due to be updated by June 30, 2026.

items.headline: DoD finds no excess suicide rate among EOD technicians
items.blurb: This DoD report to the House Armed Services Committee on explosive ordnance disposal personnel found no statistical evidence of a higher suicide rate in 2020-2024. None of the seven EOD suicide cases had a recorded PTSD or TBI diagnosis. It reviews blast and TBI risk literature and lists support options, but with numbers this small, read it as reassurance with caveats rather than a clean bill of health.
